title: Anthropic is finding bugs faster than Microsoft can fix them
gist: Internal Microsoft recordings and documents obtained by ProPublica show Anthropic's Mythos model found 90 critical and 141 important SharePoint bugs in April alone, leaving roughly 50 Microsoft employees in a 'mad dash' before a May 31 date when engineers assumed adversaries would have equivalent tooling. Microsoft's July 14 Patch Tuesday shipped over 600 fixes, triple June's record, while ~300 moderate-severity bugs stay queued—despite Mythos's ability to chain low-severity flaws into high-severity attacks.

insights.claim: In April alone Mythos uncovered 90 critical and 141 important bugs in SharePoint, and found even more in the first half of May, leaving Microsoft engineers in what a manager called a mad dash to close the gap.
insights.speaker: ProPublica
insights.so_what: A single product line generating 231 high-severity findings in one month quantifies the new baseline defect-discovery rate that every software vendor must now staff against.
insights.locator: One slide in that day’s presentation showed

insights.claim: Microsoft's July 14 Patch Tuesday released fixes for more than 600 bugs, blowing past June's more-than-200 all-time high, with only seven categorized as low or moderate severity.
insights.speaker: ProPublica
insights.so_what: A 3x month-over-month jump in patch volume at the world's largest software vendor is the hardest public evidence that the AI bug-discovery shock is real and already landing.
insights.quote: Well folks. Here we are. The bug apocalypse has fully descended upon us,
insights.locator: In June, it released patches for more than 200 bugs

insights.claim: Since Microsoft began using Mythos earlier this year it has collectively found hundreds of critical or important bugs in Microsoft 365, Teams, and the Copilot AI tool, and as of mid-May most had yet to be patched.
insights.speaker: ProPublica
insights.so_what: The exposure spans Microsoft's core enterprise franchise, not one legacy product—systemic risk to the productivity stack most large organizations depend on.
insights.locator: One document noted that, since the company started using Mythos

insights.claim: The SharePoint team was projected to be busy for months, working critical bugs first, important ones in August, and only then starting on roughly 300 moderate bugs.
insights.speaker: ProPublica
insights.so_what: A published multi-month backlog with 300 moderate bugs deferred defines a long, quantified window of known-but-unfixed exposure for SharePoint customers.
insights.locator: The internal Microsoft presentation and accompanying slides predicted

insights.claim: Microsoft acknowledged to ProPublica that the overall volume of bugs will not be plateauing for a bit, while saying it has invested heavily in people and AI-powered triage that scales.
insights.speaker: ProPublica
insights.so_what: Vendor guidance that the flood continues means sustained elevated patch-management cost for every enterprise IT budget, not a one-time spike.
insights.locator: Microsoft told ProPublica that the overall volume of bugs

insights.claim: Microsoft engineering manager Hans Andersen told staff that May 31 was considered the day when the rest of the world would have caught up, giving them roughly two weeks of privileged access to do as much good as possible.
insights.speaker: ProPublica
insights.so_what: A specific internal date for capability parity shows firms are now doing explicit time-boxed risk planning around AI diffusion—an emerging category of strategic planning.
insights.quote: is considered the day when the rest of the world will have caught up.
insights.locator: Please, please, please if your org has any April bugs

insights.claim: Engineers on the call articulated the implication bluntly—that if equivalent capability released on June 1, adversaries would have Microsoft's bugs by June 2—and colleagues agreed.
insights.speaker: ProPublica
insights.so_what: The defenders' own assumption is near-instant offensive parity, which means any patch backlog converts directly into adversary opportunity.
insights.quote: So basically you’re saying if it’s released on June 1, then on June 2 the adversaries will have our bugs?
insights.locator: The engineers on the call poked at that assertion

insights.claim: The Five Eyes intelligence alliance—the US, Australia, Canada, New Zealand and the UK—issued an unusual joint statement in late June warning the defensive window would close within months, but the Microsoft records suggest the reckoning may already be here.
insights.speaker: ProPublica
insights.so_what: When five governments issue a joint warning and internal corporate evidence says they were already late, assume the offensive-capability timeline is running ahead of public estimates.
insights.locator: In late June, the international alliance of intelligence agencies

insights.claim: Anthropic gave Mythos access to roughly 50 full-time Microsoft employees with the stated goal to harden critical services before publicly available models catch up.
insights.speaker: ProPublica
insights.so_what: Fifty seats is a tiny defensive deployment against a global attack surface—the asymmetry between privileged defensive access and eventual open offensive access is stark.
insights.locator: According to the slides that accompanied the May internal presentation

insights.claim: Some hackers have already tapped AI to automate attacks and appear to be using Mythos-like technology to find and exploit weaknesses, though no specific Mythos-identified bug is confirmed exploited.
insights.speaker: ProPublica
insights.so_what: Offensive adoption is already observable in the wild—the parity question is about degree, not whether it happens.
insights.locator: It’s unclear whether hackers have exploited any specific bug

insights.claim: When a staffer took comfort that adversaries lack Microsoft's source code, colleagues corrected him: portions of Microsoft's code have fallen into hackers' hands over the years.
insights.speaker: ProPublica
insights.so_what: Source-code secrecy provides no durable defense against AI scanning—removes the main argument that closed-source vendors are structurally safer.
insights.quote: But they’ve got source code. It’s out there.
insights.locator: During the May meeting, one staffer appeared to take comfort

themes.theme: Triage is mispriced in the chaining era

insights.claim: Mythos can chain together a string of bugs that build on one another, so the low- and moderate-severity vulnerabilities left unpatched could enable devastating attacks.
insights.speaker: ProPublica
insights.so_what: Chaining invalidates the independence assumption behind severity scoring—the deferred backlog carries far more risk than its ratings imply.
insights.locator: But that strategy carries its own risk

insights.claim: Vinh Nguyen, Anthropic senior technical adviser, CFR senior fellow for AI and former NSA chief AI officer, argues four chained low-level flaws can equal a high severity and that Microsoft's current triage strategy may be underpricing risk.
insights.speaker: ProPublica
insights.so_what: A former NSA AI chief publicly saying the largest software vendor is underpricing risk is a strong signal that CVSS-style severity models need repricing industry-wide.
insights.quote: If you’re Microsoft, the current triage strategy may be underpricing risks.
insights.locator: The problem now is that you can chain four low-level flaws

insights.claim: Microsoft's internal presentation did not mention chaining at all, though a spokesperson said the technique has long been considered part of vulnerability assessment and risk analysis.
insights.speaker: ProPublica
insights.so_what: The gap between the public position and what the internal deck actually covered is the tell that chaining is not operationally embedded in triage.
insights.locator: The company presentation did not mention chaining

insights.claim: Nguyen argues companies must staff to develop and test patches across the entire severity spectrum rather than shunting low-risk flaws aside, comparing it to a cyber ER that needs doctors treating minor wounds that could later turn deadly.
insights.speaker: ProPublica
insights.so_what: Full-spectrum patching implies a large step-change in security headcount and automation spend—directly bullish for AI-powered remediation tooling.
insights.quote: The patients are coming in fast and furious.
insights.locator: Given the new realities of the AI age

insights.claim: Microsoft conceded that AI systems are making it rethink whether flaws previously rated low or moderate should be upgraded, and that the whole industry is watching how drastic the change will be.
insights.speaker: ProPublica
insights.so_what: An admission that severity taxonomies may need revision foreshadows a re-rating of historical vulnerability data and compliance baselines.
insights.locator: Microsoft told ProPublica it’s “always going to be reevaluating

insights.claim: The Microsoft Security Response Center has been perennially understaffed, already fielding hundreds or thousands of reports a month and pushed to its limits even before the AI-identified bug crush.
insights.speaker: ProPublica
insights.so_what: A pre-existing capacity deficit means the AI shock lands on an already-saturated system—expect longer mean-time-to-patch and more exploited-before-fixed incidents.
insights.locator: Although the volume of vulnerabilities has grown over the years

insights.claim: Former employees say the center's size reflects a corporate philosophy in which plugging security holes is a cost center while making new products is a profit center, so Microsoft is loath to tie up its best engineers on patches.
insights.speaker: ProPublica
insights.so_what: Security underinvestment is an incentive-structure problem, not a capability problem—it will not self-correct without external pressure or liability.
insights.locator: The size of the center reflects Microsoft’s corporate philosophy

insights.claim: Microsoft's users are particularly exposed because its ubiquity makes it a lucrative target and many products contain decades-old legacy code carrying unaddressed flaws and technical debt.
insights.speaker: ProPublica
insights.so_what: Legacy code is where AI scanning yields the highest hit rate—vendors with the longest codebase history face the largest AI-era liability.
insights.locator: Microsoft’s users may be particularly vulnerable

insights.claim: Andersen characterized the findings as not profound and exotic but real, and said a lot of them are exploitable.
insights.speaker: ProPublica
insights.so_what: Ordinary-but-exploitable is the worst combination: easy for adversaries to weaponize once the same tooling is available.
insights.quote: They’re not profound and exotic, but they’re real,
insights.locator: As of mid-May, most of them had yet to be patched

insights.claim: The remediation challenge extends to the entire software industry and to open-source code that underpins Internet infrastructure and is largely maintained by volunteers, including code inside Microsoft's own products.
insights.speaker: ProPublica
insights.so_what: Volunteer-maintained open source has no capacity to absorb an AI-scale bug flood—the systemic weak point of the entire software supply chain.
insights.locator: But the challenge of fixing the flood of newly found bugs

insights.claim: J. Michael Daniel, former cybersecurity adviser to Barack Obama and president of the Cyber Threat Alliance, says nobody has figured out how to deal with this and everyone is casting around for what to do.
insights.speaker: ProPublica
insights.so_what: No established playbook exists at the policy level either—regulatory and standards responses are likely to be reactive and disruptive when they arrive.
insights.quote: Nobody has really figured out how to deal with this, and everybody is casting around for what they need to do,
insights.locator: Open source software underpins Internet infrastructure

insights.claim: Vulnerability data scientist Ben Edwards says the industry was already handling intense volume before AI—drinking from a garden hose on the jet setting—and now faces a fire hose that existing teams may not be able to handle.
insights.speaker: ProPublica
insights.so_what: Frames the capacity question precisely: teams sized for the prior regime are structurally inadequate, creating a durable demand pull for automated remediation.
insights.quote: It was like drinking from a garden hose on the jet setting before, and now it’s like drinking from a fire hose,
insights.locator: Ben Edwards, a data scientist who specializes

insights.claim: Project Glasswing gave Mythos access to select organizations making software used by people, companies, and governments worldwide, explicitly to fix vulnerabilities before adversarial governments like China obtain similar tools for espionage and sabotage.
insights.speaker: ProPublica
insights.so_what: A private lab is running what amounts to a national-security remediation program on a self-set timeline—an unprecedented concentration of defensive initiative outside government.
insights.locator: The tech giant was racing to fix weaknesses in its code
